Eggs of the Masked trogon (Trogon personatus) placed in an incubator set to a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after a period of approximately 17.7 days [ab = approximately 17.7 days]. This incubation duration aligns well with findings for other trogon species of comparable body size, reflecting the energetically demanding yet carefully regulated embryonic development within the altricial bird egg. The newly hatched nestlings emerge with a very modest body mass; the neonatal wet weight is approximately 7.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.2 grams]. This low hatchling mass, typical of altricial chicks, represents a small fraction of the ultimate adult size and underscores the critical role of sustained biparental provisioning during the subsequent nestling phase. The precise thermal conditions during this early developmental window appear to exert a strong influence on the timing of hatching, with the 36 °C incubation temperature representing a likely optimal condition for this montane forest species.

At a controlled ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the resting metabolic rate of the Masked trogon was measured at 150.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 150.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This basal oxygen consumption value was recorded from post-absorptive, resting adults under thermoneutral conditions placed inside a sealed respirometry chamber. The measurement reflects the species' basal maintenance costs and provides a crucial reference point for comparative studies of metabolic scaling among Neotropical birds. Interestingly, the recorded rate is somewhat higher than what might be predicted based solely on the adult body mass of this species, a discrepancy that may be linked to the energetic demands of living in high-altitude cloud forest environments. Field observations indicate that these trogons often maintain a high body temperature even during nocturnal rest, suggesting that a consistently elevated metabolic rate is a key physiological adaptation to their cool, humid habitat. This finding corresponds closely with metabolic data from other Trogonidae.

Females of the Masked trogon attain an ultimate adult wet weight of 64.7 grams [Wwi = 64.7 grams], a body size that appears to be close to the maximum capacity for this species within its high-elevation range. This ultimate wet weight, characteristic of reproductively mature females, is reached gradually during the first year of life through a sustained period of somatic growth and feather development. The body mass is consistent with the general pattern observed in the Trogonidae, where females are often slightly heavier than males, likely an adaptation linked to the energetic costs of egg production and extended incubation duties. The species' relatively moderate body mass, compared to some larger lowland trogons, is thought to be an adaptation to the cooler thermal conditions and potentially lower prey availability of its montane habitat. This mass also sets the stage for the demands of reproduction, as the female must divert a significant proportion of her energy budget toward producing a clutch of eggs that may weigh nearly a quarter of her own body mass.

Maintained at a steady environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the species demonstrates a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 12.3 years [am = approximately 12.3 years]. This longevity estimate is derived from long-term mark-recapture studies within a protected Andean cloud forest reserve and represents the oldest documented individual. Such a lifespan is comparatively extended for a bird of its body mass, suggesting that the trogon's life-history strategy is geared toward high adult survival rather than high annual fecundity. The energetic cost of this survival is reflected in the elevated basal metabolic rate measured under the same thermal conditions. The trogon's lifespan sets a temporal framework for its reproductive career; under those same conditions of 40 °C, the time since birth at first brood is observed to be approximately 1.5 years [tR = approximately 1.5 years] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delay in first reproduction is a common strategy among long-lived tropical birds, allowing ample time for territory acquisition, pair-bond formation, and the development of proficient foraging skills.
